title: Server-Side DPoP and Token Exchange in Spring Security 7
gist: A technical walk-through for teams running their own OAuth identity provider: Spring Authorization Server has merged into Spring Security 7 under the same Maven coordinates, making DPoP sender-constrained tokens (RFC 9449) and Token Exchange (RFC 8693) production-ready in one module, with upgrade traps such as DPoP verification becoming opt-in in 7.1.

insights.claim: Spring Authorization Server, standalone since 2020 and GA since November 2022, moved into Spring Security 7.0 under the same Maven groupId and artifactId, so moving off the 1.5.x line is a version bump rather than an artifact swap.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Agnihotri
insights.so_what: Java identity teams get one module, one version and one release-notes stream to track, lowering the upgrade burden.

insights.claim: Spring's November 2025 release train shipped Spring Framework 7.0 on November 13, Spring Security 7.0 on November 17 and Spring Boot 4.0 on November 20, with Spring Security 7.1.0 following in June 2026 and 7.1.1 in August 2026.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Agnihotri
insights.so_what: Release timeline for planning Spring Boot 4 migrations.

insights.claim: In Boot 4 the authorization-server starter gained a security- prefix, so spring-boot-starter-oauth2-authorization-server is deprecated in favor of spring-boot-starter-security-oauth2-authorization-server, with both still published through 4.1.1.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Agnihotri
insights.so_what: The only genuine artifact rename in the migration affects teams using the Boot starter.

insights.claim: Spring Security 7 charges a baseline migration tax unrelated to new OAuth features: and() is removed from the HttpSecurity builder, Jackson 3 replaces Jackson 2, and JWT-decoder defaults change; a team current on 6.5 deprecations can plan roughly one sprint.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Agnihotri
insights.so_what: Budget the baseline migration separately from feature adoption.

insights.claim: JwtTypeValidator.jwt() requires the typ header to be JWT or absent, so tokens with another typ such as the RFC 9068 at+jwt access-token type fail validation by default after the upgrade unless a validator allowing it is registered.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Agnihotri
insights.so_what: Audit issued and accepted token types before upgrading to avoid authentication failures in production.
insights.locator: The guide does not spell out two things

insights.claim: Teams persisting OAuth2Authorization objects with Spring's Jackson modules must move registration from SecurityJackson2Modules to SecurityJacksonModules, or deserialization of previously persisted authorization state will break.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Agnihotri
insights.so_what: A data-compatibility risk for stored authorizations; test against existing database state.
insights.locator: Second, if you persist OAuth2Authorization objects

insights.claim: In Spring Security 7.1 resource-server DPoP verification became opt-in via an explicit .dPoP() DSL call, so applications that relied on the auto-applied verification in 6.5 or 7.0, including Boot default autoconfiguration, silently stop enforcing DPoP after upgrading until the call is added.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Agnihotri
insights.so_what: An upgrade can silently weaken security posture; verify DPoP enforcement in tests after moving to 7.1.
insights.locator: Verification Is Now Stock at the Resource Server

insights.claim: DPoP (RFC 9449) constrains an access token to a key the client holds by having the client sign a short-lived proof JWT per request, so a stolen token is inert without the private key.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Agnihotri
insights.so_what: Sender-constrained tokens reduce the impact of token theft, a standard mitigation for bearer-token replay.

insights.claim: Spring does not implement the RFC 9449 server-chosen nonce challenge as of Spring Security 7.1.1 (no DPoP-Nonce header, no use_dpop_nonce handling, no nonce claim validator); teams whose threat model needs it must build the mechanism themselves.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Agnihotri
insights.so_what: A gap for high-security deployments; the nonce is only a SHOULD in the RFC, which may explain the omission.

insights.claim: From Spring Security 6.5.12 / 7.1.1 the DPoP jti replay check is a pluggable DPoPProofReplayValidator whose default in-memory cache (100,000 entries) only works in a single-node setup, so clustered deployments must supply a distributed cache such as Redis or Hazelcast; earlier versions used a hard-coded thousand-entry cache.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Agnihotri
insights.so_what: Multi-node IdPs running DPoP with the default cache leave a replay gap across nodes.
insights.locator: Second, there is the replay cache

insights.claim: Spring automatically binds the access token to the proof key through cnf.jkt (RFC 7638 thumbprint) and binds refresh tokens for public clients to the DPoP key, so these require no configuration.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Agnihotri
insights.so_what: Key binding for SPAs and native apps comes built in; only an accidental token customizer overwriting cnf is a risk.

insights.claim: RFC 8693 Token Exchange replaces the bespoke service-account swap many in-house IdPs carry with a standard grant; Spring added it in Authorization Server 1.3.0-M3 (March 2024) and it is in the 7.x module.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Agnihotri
insights.so_what: A standard grant reduces custom auth code and its audit surface.
insights.locator: Token Exchange Without the Bespoke Plumbing

insights.claim: Sending only a subject_token yields an impersonation token with no act claim, while adding an actor_token produces a delegation token that preserves both identities, with nested act claims recording a multi-hop chain; delegation is the right choice for audit and service-to-service calls.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Agnihotri
insights.so_what: Delegation tokens give auditable who-acted-for-whom trails, relevant for compliance and agent systems.
insights.locator: The exchange matters most for the two semantics

insights.claim: The token-exchange grant is not enabled by default per client: the RegisteredClient must declare AuthorizationGrantType.TOKEN_EXCHANGE or the request is rejected with unsupported_grant_type.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Agnihotri
insights.so_what: Per-client opt-in limits exposure when rolling out.
insights.locator: The grant is not enabled by default per client

insights.claim: A token-exchange endpoint should only reduce authority, and one that can be leveraged to obtain broader scope than the subject token holds is a privilege-escalation bug; Spring supplies the grant and customizer hook but does not stop an exchange that widens scope, so the OAuth2TokenCustomizer is security-critical code needing its own tests.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Agnihotri
insights.so_what: The security of exchange rests on custom narrowing logic; require code review and tests for it.
insights.locator: One principle is worth holding on to

themes.theme: DPoP plus Token Exchange for service chains and agents

insights.claim: Combining a DPoP-bound subject token with token exchange yields a narrowed, audience-restricted token re-bound to the calling service's key with the actor recorded, so no hop holds a replayable credential for a service it does not call.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Agnihotri
insights.so_what: This is the standards-based pattern for propagating constrained authority in microservice and agentic architectures.
insights.locator: The Pattern That Needs Both DPoP and Token Exchange

insights.claim: Service meshes and agentic systems keep reinventing constrained-authority propagation with ad hoc header passing, and Spring Security 7 is the first official Spring surface where RFC 8693 and RFC 9449 ship together.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Agnihotri
insights.so_what: Agent-identity and authorization tooling may converge on these standards, favoring platforms with native support.
insights.locator: This is the shape that modern service meshes and agentic systems

insights.claim: For production rollout, resource-server .dPoP() support should be deployed before issuing DPoP-bound tokens, DPoP enabled per client registration rather than globally, bearer and DPoP tokens allowed to coexist in a dual-stack window, and DPoP and the token-exchange grant advertised in authorization-server metadata.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Agnihotri
insights.so_what: Sequencing reduces outage risk when moving a client fleet to sender-constrained tokens.
insights.locator: The production rollout has its own decisions
